entries.notes: Also 'high' for things, not just people.
Short in height. Also 'low' for things.
Invariable: same form for masculine and feminine.
Dark-haired; can also mean dark-skinned or tanned.
With 'ser' it means boring; with 'estar' it means bored.
Of a person: open-minded or outgoing.
Of a person: reserved or closed-off.
False friend — not 'sympathetic'.
With 'ser', cheerful by nature; with 'estar', happy right now.
Plural 'los padres' means parents, not just fathers.
Masculine plural covering both parents.
Plural 'los hijos' means children (sons and daughters).
Plural 'los abuelos' means grandparents.
Plural 'los hermanos' means siblings, or brothers specifically; context decides.
Plural 'los nietos' means grandchildren.
Means both 'wife' and 'woman'; 'esposa' is the more formal word for wife.
Plural 'los tíos' means aunts and uncles. In Spain 'tío/tía' is also very common slang for 'guy' or 'mate'.
'Todos' agrees with the noun: todos los días, but todas las semanas.
'Al' is 'a' + 'el' contracted.
Masculine despite ending in -a: el día, todos los días.
Time as in an occasion: una vez, dos veces. Not clock time.
With a clock time it becomes 'de': a las ocho de la mañana.
'La mañana' is the morning; 'mañana' on its own means tomorrow.
Masculine despite ending in -a.
In Spain 'la tarde' runs until about 8 or 9 pm, later than English 'afternoon'.
Literally 'to wash the teeth'. Spanish uses 'los dientes', not 'mis dientes'; the reflexive pronoun already says whose.
entries.flagged: Multi-word reflexive: the headword ends in 'dientes', not '-se', so the validator's reflexive check may need to allow this.

entries.notes: 'Al' is 'a' + 'el'. See 'ir' for the conjugation.
In Spain 'comer' means to have lunch specifically (the main midday meal); 'almorzar' is less common.
Understood in Spain but 'comer' is the everyday word for lunch there.
'Del' is 'de' + 'el'. See 'salir' for the conjugation.
Plural 'los dientes'.
For identity, traits, and origin: mi hermano es alto. Compare 'estar'.
For location and temporary states: está aburrido = he is bored. Compare 'ser'.
Me llamo Doliver = my name is Doliver.
'To love' for people: te quiero. For things it means to want.
Days are lowercase and the week starts on Monday. 'Los lunes' means on Mondays; 'el lunes' means this Monday.
Unlike Monday to Friday, the plural adds -s: los sábados.
Months are lowercase. Dates go number first: el 15 de enero.
Becomes 'un' before a masculine noun (un hermano) and 'una' before a feminine one.
Written as one word, with an accent. 16 to 19 and 21 to 29 all follow this one-word pattern.
Becomes 'veintiún' before a masculine noun: veintiún años.
From 31 upwards numbers are two words joined by 'y': treinta y uno, cuarenta y dos.
Exactly 100. From 101 it becomes 'ciento': ciento uno, ciento cincuenta.
Irregular: not 'cincocientos'. Agrees in gender: quinientas mujeres.
Irregular: not 'sietecientos'.
Irregular: not 'nuevecientos'.
No article: mil, not 'un mil'. Does not change for gender.
Used as an adjective or a noun: es muy dormilón. The accent drops in the feminine and plural.
entries.flagged: Typed as 'dormilión'; assumed the class word is 'dormilón'.

entries.notes: As a trait, someone with healthy habits; 'estar sano' is to be in good health right now.
Colloquial; also used as a noun (un fiestero).
The feminine adds -a even though the masculine ends in a consonant. Also the noun 'worker'.
Someone who eats a lot. The accent drops in the feminine and plural.
entries.flagged: Typed as 'comiión'; assumed the class word is 'comilón'.

entries.notes: Same form for both genders despite ending in -a: un chico deportista, una chica deportista. Also the noun 'athlete'.
Of a person, a homebody. Of things it means homemade (comida casera); as a noun, el casero is a landlord.
Also the adjective 'scientific'.
Anyone who cooks for a living; a head chef is 'el chef' or 'el jefe de cocina'.
Same form for both genders: el estudiante, la estudiante.
The feminine adds -a even though the masculine ends in a consonant: diseñadora.
Ends in -a but is masculine too: el periodista, la periodista.
In Spain the everyday word for any teacher, not only a university professor. The feminine adds -a: profesora.
The feminine adds -a even though the masculine ends in a consonant: traductora.
The word in Spain; 'mesero' is common in Latin America.
Same form for both genders: el deportista, la deportista. Also the adjective 'sporty', listed separately.
Same form for both genders: el comercial, la comercial. Also the adjective 'commercial'.
Nouns ending in -dad are feminine: la universidad, la ciudad.
The newspaper itself and the company that makes it: trabaja en un periódico.
In Spain a bar serves coffee and breakfast as much as drinks, so it is often closer to a café.
In Spain a primary or secondary school is usually 'el colegio' (el cole); escuela is common for specialist schools, as in escuela de idiomas.
One person's office, or a study at home; a larger shared office is 'la oficina'.
